summary: Describes EAP-pwd, an Extensible Authentication Protocol method that authenticates with a shared password, even a weak one an attacker could guess from a dictionary. The key exchange resists active, passive and dictionary attacks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: EAP-pwd lets a peer and server use a shared password to authenticate and derive session keys. Captured messages do not let an attacker test a dictionary of passwords offline, but repeated online guesses remain possible.

questions: how does eap-pwd resist dictionary attacks
what is the eap-pwd method type
subtitle: An EAP password exchange designed to limit offline guessing from captured traffic.

tldr.problem: People often use passwords that attackers can guess from a dictionary, so a password exchange should not expose data that enables offline testing of guesses.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-pwd runs Identity, Commit and Confirm exchanges; the peers derive a Password Element and exchange masked group values to establish shared keys.
tldr.outcome: The design limits an active attack to testing one password guess per run, but does not prevent repeated online guesses. RFC 5931 is Informational and RFC 8146 updates it per the supplied metadata.

today: RFC 5931 is an Informational RFC published in August 2010 and has been updated by RFC 8146. It describes EAP-pwd and notes that repeated online password guessing remains possible.

sections.title: The Password Authentication Problem
sections.content:
EAP-pwd is an Extensible Authentication Protocol method for password-based authentication and key exchange. It is designed to work even when the shared password has low entropy and an attacker knows the set of likely passwords.

The RFC's goals include resistance to passive, active and dictionary attacks, plus forward secrecy. It defines dictionary resistance so that an attacker can learn whether a single guess is correct only through an interaction with an honest participant.
sections.plainLanguage: EAP-pwd uses a shared password to authenticate the peer and server and derive a secret. Its design aims to prevent captured traffic from supporting repeated offline password guesses.

sections.title: Groups, Password Element and Keys
sections.content:
The method uses a cryptographic group based on finite-field or elliptic-curve cryptography. The peers derive a Password Element (PWE) deterministically from the password, identities, token and ciphersuite; to an attacker without the password, the selected element should appear random.

The RFC defines the random function as HMAC-SHA256 with a 32-octet zero key. Each side must generate quality secret random values, and the successful exchange derives a Master Key that is expanded into a 512-bit MSK and a 512-bit EMSK.
sections.plainLanguage: Both participants use the password and agreed identities to calculate the same value. Fresh secret random numbers help them create shared keys without sending the password.

sections.title: Identity, Commit and Confirm Exchanges
sections.content:
In the Identity exchange, the server sends its identity, a ciphersuite, an anti-clogging token and a password-processing method; the peer acknowledges these and supplies its identity. Both sides then derive the Password Element.

In the Commit exchange, each side sends a scalar and group element derived from secret random values. In the Confirm exchange, each side sends verification data tied to the shared calculation and the ciphersuite; matching values allow the exchange to complete.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers first exchange identities and agree on parameters. They then exchange values prepared with secret random numbers and confirm they derived the same secret.

sections.title: Packet Format and Fragmentation
sections.content:
EAP-pwd uses method type 52. Its header includes a code, identifier, length, an L bit, an M bit and a field identifying the Identity, Commit or Confirm exchange.

Messages larger than the available EAP size can be fragmented. The first fragment indicates the total length, all but the last mark that more fragments follow, and the receiver acknowledges each fragment before the sender continues; without a known lower-layer MTU, the threshold is 1020 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: EAP-pwd labels each packet with its exchange type. Large messages are split into fragments, and each fragment is acknowledged before the next is sent.

sections.title: Attack Limits and Security Properties
sections.content:
The RFC explains that an active attacker can test at most one password guess during a single attack run. Fresh random values also mean that learning the password later does not reveal keys from earlier successful runs.

The protocol does not prevent repeated online guessing. Implementations SHOULD use a sufficiently large password pool and SHOULD take measures such as refusing attempts after a threshold of failures; the RFC specifies no threshold or waiting period. The Identity and Commit exchanges are not encrypted, and the peer and server identities are visible.
sections.plainLanguage: The method limits each active attack to one password guess, but an attacker can make repeated online attempts. The RFC recommends large password pools and implementation countermeasures against repeated failures.
